subsubtopic: UNION WORK-SHARING PRACTICES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity dealing with the unfair practice within the present work-sharing programs of certain unions. Contrary to the statement of the Minister of Labour regarding this work-sharing program, it has come to my attention that a great number of unions, including the UAW, are indeed making it obligatory for their membership to work beyond the number of prescribed hours in a working week, thereby curtailing considerably potential work opportunities for tens of thousands of unemployed, many of whom already have had extensive experience in their respective fields. That this House instruct the Minister of Labour to acquaint himself forthwith with this unfair practice and take any necessary action in order to rectify the work-sharing problem now being faced by a great number of unemployed.

subsubtopic: SALE OF CAN DU REACTOR TO ARGENTINA-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ALLEGED PAY-OFFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. He will remember yesterday I brought up the matter of the media revelations respecting one Jose Ben Gelbard, an ex-minister in the government of Argentina, who is alleged to have been the prime recipient of Canadian taxpayer's money in respect of an AECL Argentine CANDU reactor pay-off.

May 20, 1977

Almost unbelievably, and I say that most advisedly, the Acting Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues who were in the House indicated that they knew nothing of that report yesterday. He indicated as well that he would take up the matter immediately and I presume call for immediate reports from his colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Department of External Affairs and the Department of the Solicitor General in regard to the RCMP investigation into this matter. That is what the Acting Prime Minister undertook yesterday in the House. I ask him to fulfil his commitment now. What has been done, what does he know about it, and can he verify these reports?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. gentleman, may I say 1 have asked for further information on the question. The Department of External Affairs has put into place an investigation in an effort to verify these allegations. On the surface, there appear to be considerable discrepancies in the reports, but I am not in a position to go into any detail. With respect to the Department of the Solicitor General, I understand that the RCM Police are still investigating these matters. I have no further comment to make. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is in the chamber and he may wish to add to or subtract from that answer.

subsubtopic: SALE OF CAN DU REACTOR TO ARGENTINA-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ALLEGED PAY-OFFS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary has to be to the Acting Prime Minister again in view of the obvious apathy that his ministerial colleague is showing in not rising in his place in this House. Obviously, the government believes or hopes that if there is no further reference to this matter, it will quietly disappear from the scene. I can assure them it is not going to disappear from the scene. Twenty-four hours ago the minister made a commitment to this House that he would indicate what he and the government are doing about this matter and to verify or comment further on these reports. That report has been available to the minister and the government for at least four days. The Financial Post is published on Monday or Tuesday of each week. It has been available here in Ottawa. It has been on the wire services. The continued evasion of the government in this matter is something that is abhorrent to us all.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one of the recommendations which was made in the Berger report dealing with the Beaufort drilling program was that Canada call together the circumpolar nations in an international conference. Before we destroy the Arctic we should at least talk to some people about how we can go about cleaning it up. 1 am wondering if the minister can advise the House whether that particular recommendation in the Berger report is now before cabinet and when we will receive a decision from the government in terms of that specific recommendation, that is, the calling of a circumpolar conference of all the polar nations around the Arctic so that we can make sure we do not do anything to the climate of this planet with oil spills in that sensitive area.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DRILLING IN BEAUFORT SEA-PROPOSED CONFERENCE OF CIRCUMPOLAR NATIONS ON ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have already stated on behalf of the government that we have taken and are taking the Berger report very seriously indeed. That is the general situation. I have had no indication that the Minister of the Environment has decided to call, in advance of those general decisions, a conference of the circumpolar nations, although it is obviously a matter of interest to the government and may very well be a proposal which can be acted upon.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: USE OF ANTI-SPALLING COMPOUNDS IN THE EXTERIOR CONCRETE SURFACES
speechtext: Is the government aware of reports that exterior concrete construction surfaces treated with anti-spalling compounds will last up to ten years longer and, in some cases, ten times longer than those surfaces not treated and, if so, is the government giving consideration to including the use of anti-spalling compounds as a protection in all construction contracts in Canada and especially those entered into by the Department of Public Works and, if not, for what reason?

speakeroldname: Mr. Alexandre Cyr (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subsubtopic: USE OF ANTI-SPALLING COMPOUNDS IN THE EXTERIOR CONCRETE SURFACES
speechtext: The Department of Public Works is not aware of any reports by established research or testing organizations on exterior concrete construction surfaces treated with anti-spalling compounds. In normal environments good quality concrete, with scientifically designed ingredients and properly installed, will last indefinitely. It would, therefore, be a waste to treat all exterior concrete with alleged anti-spalling compounds in all construction contracts in Canada. In particularly corrosive environments special precautions are usually taken, but such situations are a small percentage of the overall.

Excise Tax

The House resumed, from Tuesday, May 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-54, to amend the Excise Tax Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, on May 17 the minister made his opening statement with regard to second reading of this bill and outlined in part those matters which are to be handled in the bill this afternoon. I would like to talk about the air travel tax to which there is now an extension so that it becomes all-encompassing. I suppose there is a case that can be made for the imposition of an air travel tax within certain limits in Canada. When the matter first came up, there was tremendous objection across the country to the formula that was proposed, which was on a percentage basis. The formula would have hit particularly people who lived long distances from central Canada.
The formula was going to be based upon the value of the ticket, and it included, at that time, frontier areas; there were no exemptions at all. That just did not wash. Even though I moved a motion at that time which substituted a dollar value which would have yielded the same amount of money, I recall the Chair ruled my amendment out of order. With the greatest respect, I think the Chair was totally wrong. The Speaker indicated that he was not going to introduce any innovations, and in any event he was going to rule against the motion I made.
Be that as it may, we have now had this air travel tax for a couple of years. It is on a fixed dollar basis and is a user-pay tax. This concept of user-pay is dearly loved by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). That is now being abandoned in a number of sectors, principally on the west coast ferries.
The tax is being applied with equal vigour across the country except in the frontier areas. What is being given back to the travelling passenger who is paying the shot is a long way from even. For instance, in Toronto there are customs preclearance facilities to go to the United States. If you try to get them in Edmonton and Calgary, you are told by the minister and his representatives that the airlines have to put up the facilities; the airlines have to charge the passengers, and therefore Edmonton and Calgary traffic has to pay an extra charge for facilities which are provided for under the $5 tax in Toronto. Is that an even hand in the handling of passengers across the country? Every international airport handling traffic to and from the United States should have preclearance facilities such as Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa, Winnipeg, Edmonton, Calgary and Vancouver.
The Minister of Transport can smile. However, if he has been listening he knows that passengers outside of Toronto-I will not speak about the mess in Montreal-are getting the
80016-30/4

May 20, 1977
Excise Tax
short end of the stick. They should have negotiated and arranged for preclearance facilities long ago. The absence of preclearance facilities in Canada gives the American lines an advantage over Canadian lines on competitive routes.
Talk about dragging their feet in Transport! Preclearance facilities in Edmonton and Calgary have been under discussion for years. The latest answer I have from the Minister of Transport is that when western Canada's "Mirabel" comes into operation in Calgary in September of this year, the facilities will exist for preclearance. For Edmonton, which has an equal demand for preclearance, it may be the fall of 1978, after the Commonwealth Games. That does not bother the minister one bit. The traffic flow into Edmonton will be somewhat less than Calgary as a result. They say that, because Calgary has more traffic than Edmonton, it should be treated differently. That is a lot of poppycock. The dice are loaded. In so far as the utilization of this air travel tax is concerned, the Department of Transport is applying it with an uneven hand.
I have been asking about the facilities in Gander from a revenue and an immigration point of view. Frankly, the minister is content to handle passengers who are flying through on a sort of cattle-pen basis. There are very inadequate temporary facilities. In so far as getting on with the job and putting in permanent facilities, Transport Canada are dragging their feet. All this is done within the comfort of headquarters in Ottawa. It does not much matter to the people who make the decision whether there is delay. If the increase is in building costs, they would not have to pay the shot. Therefore, it is an easy decision to defer. However, from the taxpayers' point of view it is a stupid decision. It costs the taxpayers from 20 to 25 per cent more, and they get less service.
I see the Minister of Transport is leaving the chamber. I just want to say to him that in this particular area there is a justifiable complaint. I hope he will take part in this debate and tell us what he proposes to do about the even application of the airport travel tax which is chargeable to all passengers in Canada. Some will get a dime's service in return and others will get their $5 worth every time they travel. The travelling public in Canada is entitled to a much better break than that.
We sometimes wonder why it is so difficult to have regional contact in Canada. We must contemplate the fact that to travel within Canada, for example from Ottawa or Toronto to Calgary or Edmonton, it costs more than flying to Europe on charter. In winter, the bulk of the Canadian population have greater access to European ski resorts than to the Rockies. Why? Canadians are being stuck, really having it rammed home, with regard to travel within their own country. There is something wrong. This problem must be worked out. This is why there is a sense of bitterness and frustration at times. The ministers should get involved and talk to those who are affected in this way.
The same principle is applied in another area. I cannot condemn it enough. The minister is now trying to even-up the situation with regard to buying tickets in Canada or buying them outside Canada. That part of it is fine. However, 1 want the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) to understand that

in utilizing these funds the Minister of Transport has to be much fairer. The changes being made in the sales tax are not all subject to criticism. The minister has taken one very salutary step. It has taken some time to get there, but I-and, I am sure, members on all sides of the House-thank the minister. I refer to the so-called small business limit which so severely affected philanthropic organizations, rehab centres and individuals partially incapacitated who produced a small volume of goods of one variety or another: they could be handicrafts, or all sorts of other things.
I do not know when the $3,000 limit was put on. One might almost say that the new $10,000 limit has merely taken care of inflation. At least it is a step in the right direction. To that extent, the minister is to be congratulated for his compassion with regard to these people and public service organizations. We hope the minister's officials will keep their minds open to further relaxation in order to get ahead of just the impact of inflation and to encourage these people to do something on their own. It is far better for an individual who has a small business to produce $15,000 or $20,000 worth of goods from which he will not derive that much income, if he can sell them without an impost of sales tax. What is the alternative? Welfare, some form of social assistance. Where does the social assistance come from? It comes from the pockets of hon. members and the taxpaying public. It is ridiculous. There is a wrong social implication to it. It is far better to encourage individuals to go out and wrestle for themselves. As a result, they would have a sense of dignity.
I have had a good deal to do with people in the social services' field in my home city. I have always found it absolutely inconceivable that the so-called principles of equity of taxation have borne down as hard on these people as they have on others. Yet there we were, trying to encourage them to some degree of self-sufficiency through rehabilitation centres to get them back on their feet. After all, one has only to engage in correspondence with the disability section of the Canada Pension Plan to see the rules which are applied there as to whether a person is disabled. It is almost a matter of, if people can breathe or stand up, they are not disabled. That section feels that if people can do some form of work-and it cannot say what form-that is the responsibility of those people, so they are denied benefits under the Canada Pension Plan for which they and their employer have paid. The government pays nothing into the Canada Pension Plan, not one blessed red cent, and the alternative for these people is to seek welfare.
The government is quite prepared to pay 50 per cent under the Canada welfare plan for the support of people who, with a little bit of initiative and some sense of personal worth, are prepared to do something. But no, we have to tax them. I think this is a strong and very compelling case which provides equity to taxpayers generally and to citizens generally. This proposal would not only maintain this type of level of exemption to take care of inflation, but it also would have an incentive, and I suggest to the minister in all sincerity that he should look at
May 20, 1977

that to see if we cannot in some way restore an incentive for partially disabled persons. I refer to blind persons and others in the same category. However, let us consider those who may suffer from heart trouble and who cannot carry on their normal work, but who can engage in some type of small production alone or in conjunction with others. I referred only to heart trouble, but it might be some other crippling disease which handicaps people, such as arthritis. There are all kinds of handicapped people. From a social point of view, I think we could use our tax system to encourage those people and to improve social benefits so they will not just be recipients of welfare, which is so soul-deadening for so many in this country.
There are many points in this legislation which my colleagues will want to talk about. I know they wish to talk about points dealing with gasoline and diesel fuel, but there is one I would like to talk about at this stage. I am sorry I did not have the correspondence I now have at the time we were discussing Bill C-55. I have here an exchange of correspondence with the minister's colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin). The reply she gave me was quite right, that the way the Customs Tariff is now worded, it would require a minor amendment to let this particular type of equipment through free of customs duty and sales tax. I am referring to spray markers. We have to be very, shall we say, simple here. It is a small matter, but very important.
I am referring to markers for agricultural aerial sprayers. Hon. members might wonder what on earth those are. Well, we have to understand what is done by aerial sprayers and what it means to western agriculture to spray pesticides or fertilizers. It is remarkable how many pilots of these aircraft there are. They have to use markers on the ground in the same way anyone here would when marking out his garden. There is one way of doing this, and that is, of course, to have a couple of persons on the ground walking along the edges of the field and marking out the lines for spraying or for fertilizing. Some people have been killed because, let us remember, these aircraft fly very low. Others, unfortunately, have been sprayed by pesticides, and they continue to be sprayed. The alternative is to use very light, brightly coloured markers.
In outlining the case to the Minister of National Revenue on March 31,1 referred to an entry at the port of Red Deer. An Alberta firm was endeavouring to bring in these markers from the United States through the port of Red Deer, but it was charged a considerable sum in customs duty and sales tax. In my letter to the Minister of National Revenue I wrote the following:
These markers are made of a special form of tissue paper and actually represent a necessary substitute for a human flagman, hitherto used and exposed to vapour spray, etc. In addition, there have been persons killed by being struck by the wheels of the low flying aircraft and there have been many near misses ... the American firm called North American Industries Incorporated of Walla Walla, Washington have been able to obtain the necessary kind of paper and put these markers on the market.
Canadian paper mills have all been canvassed, but none of them has been prepared to manufacture a similar type of paper in the rather limited quantity which is needed to supply
Excise Tax
the Canadian market. The market may grow as time goes on, but at the present time there is just no one who is prepared to manufacture this type of tissue paper. However, combining the American requirements and the Canadian requirements makes it a viable operation. Unfortunately, under the Customs Tariff classification there is duty and tax. It seems to me that since this commodity is not manufactured in Canada, and since there is little likelihood it will be because of the limited market, Canadian agriculture again has to take it in the neck.
The costs are higher for Canadian producers. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) and hon. members from other areas where large-scale agriculture is the order of the day will readily support me when I say that I think there is a case here for submission to the Minister of Finance for relief from the customs duty on this item. After all, we went through the Customs Tariff the other day and there are some items which are really sophisticated. I think a better case can be made for these aerial markers than for the free importation of frogs legs, for example, and there are a number of other things which are rather sophisticated in the Customs Tariff.
Therefore, a matter of this kind is worthy of consideration, and I submit it to the minister for relief from customs duties. If that is done, then we can make a case for relief from sales tax. That is what is relevant today. They would of course, both be relevant to customs and sales tax. So many commodities in agriculture, because they go into the production of food, are relieved from customs and sales tax, and I think this is a particularly good case.
Mr. Speaker, I think I have spoken long enough. This afternoon other hon. members will be raising various points. We will be able to deal with these matters later in committee of the whole. For those things which have not been done, then, of course, second reading procedure provides the opportunity for remarks or exhortations to the minister. I hope my colleagues will make some good suggestions.
This is not a subject that has the greatest sex appeal as far as hon. members and the public are concerned. They do not realize that often in debates of this kind their pocketbooks are either being relieved of money or, through the representations of hon. members, relieved of an unnecessary impost of taxes. I think this is one of the purposes of discussion of a tax bill. I hope we can carry on and by the end of the afternoon finish with this bill.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us, Bill C-54, is often regarded as a rather routine piece of legislation. It is true that with the exception of the air transportation tax, its provisions are more or less technical rather than of a substantive nature. That does not mean that this bill is unimportant or that it will have little impact on the average Canadian. In that connection, I think it is important that we get on the record the amount of money that we are actually referring to as far as revenue is concerned at the federal level as a result of the taxes that are imposed within the act that we are proposing to amend today.

May 20, 1977
Excise Tax
Today I refer hon. members to the publication entitled "Public Accounts of Canada, 1976, Volume 1, Summary Review of Financial Statements." At page 5-3 it is pointed out that under excise taxes the sales tax alone yielded $3,365 million, or 11.5 per cent of the total federal government revenue, in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1976. The next item which comes in the same general category is oil export charges, which amount to $1,062,900,000, or 3.6 per cent of the total federal government revenue. Other taxes that come under the general heading of excise tax amount to $437.7 million, or 1.5 per cent of the total federal government revenue. Special excise tax on gasoline, which most of us are very sensitive to, amounted to $425.1 million, or 1.5 per cent of the total federal government revenue.
Hon. members might be interested in page 5-6 of the same report. We find there that not only is there sales tax of roughly $3.3 billion, but the other excise taxes on such things as cigarettes, tobacco and cigars, yield $369 million; on jewelry, watches and ornaments, $32.5 million; matches and lighters, $2.8 million; wines, $12 million; and sundry items, about $19 million.
I mention those figures because I think it is important in dealing with this bill today that we realize the magnitude of the revenue that comes out of the legislation we are now proposing to question. Even in this bill of only 12 pages and 20 clauses, the government demonstrates a remarkable knack for convoluting reason and for adopting policies that are in many ways almost 180 degrees off dead centre.
In the case of the air transportation tax to which the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) referred, the government has managed to take a regressive step, when bold initiatives are needed. It has somehow managed to devise a tax on tourism at a time when our need for the tourist dollar has never been greater. In this bill the minister is proposing that we siphon an additional $15 million to $17 million from air travellers this year. It is perhaps an understandable, or at least a predictable measure, with Mirabel having lost $56 million in its first year of operation and being projected to lose another $56 million this year.
It is perhaps predictable that the government gets on to this user-pay concept when we realize they have tied up $110 million in federal funds in the still-born Pickering airport project in the Toronto area. In short, it is not surprising that the government would rather covet this form of additional revenue. In its present form, the tax, we understand, generated about $61 million between April, 1976, and February, 1977. This year it is expected that the tax will raise something like $66 million. Perhaps at committee of the whole the minister will be able to give us more precise figures on how much he anticipates in revenue from this tax alone.
Before the proposal becomes law by passage of this bill, I think we have to consider whether it is right to be extending this tax to travellers who purchase tickets outside of Canada. Surely we should be asking that question. Of the 2.3 million passengers the minister says will come under this new tax, more than 2 million are foreign visitors to Canada. That is the
[Mr. Stevens.)
number of visitors to Canada who arrived by air last year, according to Statistics Canada. To put it plainly and simply, this tax is a levy on tourism, despite the minister's rather oblique reference to "travellers who use Canadian airports."
That the minister should propose such a tax when our national travel account is in a deficit is myopic indeed. Surely hon. members do not have to be reminded that last year the over-all travel account in Canada registered a deficit of $1.2 billion, 63 per cent greater than in 1975 despite the major attraction of the Montreal Olympics.
It is a dismal record and one which should command the government's concerted efforts to rectify it. Since 1971, our over-all travel deficit has widened five-fold; that is, our travel deficit in 1976 was more than 500 per cent greater than that of 1971. Anyone wishing to confirm for himself this drift from a deficit of $202 million in 1971 to $1.2 billion in 1976 should look no further than table 25 on page 61 of the minister's own "Economic Review" that was tabled recently in this House. I strongly urge the minister to read that report which his department prepared for him and to reconsider his proposal to tax foreign visitors who use our airports. To tax tourism- however marginally-in the face of deficits like these is shortsighted and insensitive. Let there be no mistake about that.
We are not suggesting that the bill will be a direct deterrent to air travellers coming to Canada. At $8 or less per person, this tax, especially when compared to international air fares from Europe and beyond, will however be one further deterrent to such tourism being expanded as far as Canada is concerned. If the bill does little to discourage tourism, it does nothing to encourage it. It is a further deterrent to tourists visiting this country; it does nothing to encourage tourism and will not help us to overcome our deficit in tourism. The bill represents another lost chance to take imaginative, positive action for remedying our critical deficits. In this context, Bill C-54 and the air transportation tax should be viewed as an incomprehensibly regressive measure. We see, here, a small, mean little step backward, whereas vision was required or leaving well enough alone would have been sufficient.
It is interesting to review the government's justification for the airport tax. In the budget brought in on June 23, 1975, former minister of finance John Turner proposed to extend the air transport tax which had originally been imposed in 1974. He said:
The increases, to be effective August 1 this year-
Meaning, 1975.
-are essential to reflect the general policy that those who benefit most directly from facilities provided by the government help to pay for them.
In other budgetary presentations, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has adopted the user-pay concept with respect to airports. Perhaps it is fair to ask users to pay, but that stops short of the real question, which is this: Has the government been prudent in operating our airports? Has it controlled airport expenditures? In short, if users or others are required to pay, must they pay for the expenditures which
May 20, 1977

have been incurred? I raise this question because I think one should be aware of some interesting figures. For example, I note that in the 1970 fiscal year our airports actually made money. On the other hand, during the last seven years, owing largely to the Department of Transport's inept, incompetent approach to airports, our airports ran up a staggering deficit which the government now asks users to make good.
If the government had shown more foresight, a little more restraint, a little less bureaucratic proclivity to indulge in the building of white elephants like Mirabel and the still-born Pickering project near Toronto, users would not have to pay a nickel and our airports would be breaking even or making a profit. Let me put some figures on record.
After paying almost $20 million in construction costs in 1970, our airports showed a deficit of $2 million. In short, they made about $18 million or more in profits from their operations in 1970. For example, Montreal's international airport, Dorval, after spending $482,000 on construction and acquisitions in that year, actually made a profit of $9 million from operations. Malton, near Toronto, made over $2 million, even after spending $6.3 million on construction and acquisitions. In short, our airports made money from operations in 1970.
Owing to this government's sheer incompetence and mismanagement, that picture changed. According to current estimates, or estimates relating to the 1978 fiscal year, it is estimated that our airports will lose $133 million. That is a colossal turnaround. In seven or eight years our airports, instead of making modest profits from operations have managed to run up enormous losses. As I said, the anticipated loss in the 1978 fiscal year will be $133 million. Therefore, is it not fair to ask if the user-pay concept is justified? Should users be asked to pay for expenditures the prudence of which is open to question? Let me emphasize that much of the $133 million anticipated loss is attributable to operational losses incurred by misadventures in airports like Mirabel.
It is anticipated that in the fiscal year previously alluded to, Mirabel is expected to lose some $56 million, but Dorval is expected to make $1.1 million. Malton makes money on its operations but loses money on construction. This year, Malton will incur a net loss of about $16 million, after having made a profit of $19 million from operations and spending about $36 million on construction. The Pickering project, of course, is a big loser, running up losses of $17 million. In short, people are not being asked to pay the $8 tax to cover the basic cost of running our airports; they are asked to pay the tax in order to make up the deficits which have been incurred by the Mirabel and Pickering developments-and that is the truth.
In our consideration of this bill we should ask this question: Is it fair to make people using Edmonton airport, Halifax airport or, say, Thunder Bay airport pay the airport tax, without making it clear to them that the tax will cover the deficit run up by Mirabel and developments like Pickering? Because that is the purpose of this bill, and let us not forget it.
We suggest the minister should consider suspending the tax in Canada at least during the tourist season, instead of extending it to foreign visitors as is now intended. I suggest such a
Excise Tax
measure might mitigate somewhat regional disparities in our air fares and encourage Canadians to take vacations in their own country, offsetting that classic rationalization for travel abroad, namely, that it is cheaper to fly to Florida from central Canada than to Newfoundland or British Columbia.
If we choose not to impose the tax, I suggest we could gain a competitive edge, slight though it may be, over those countries which impose such taxes. This factor is especially important when we consider the balance of our travel account vis-a-vis the United States whose citizens are coming to Canada in declining numbers for the third consecutive year. Last year alone the number of United States visitors decreased by two million: fewer visitors came to this country again this year, and please bear in mind that this year we do not have the attraction of the 1976 Olympics.
There are many reasons for this decline. An important one, I suggest, is rising prices in this country. Our travel account with the United States having turned around from a surplus of $132 million in 1974 to a deficit of $610 million last year, it is time for the government to direct its energies to making travel in Canada more attractive and less expensive. We should be pursuing incentives for tourism, not taxes on tourism.
Recently I was talking with some tourist-oriented businessmen in Niagara Falls. Frankly, I was astonished at the difference they were able to show me between taxation on the United States side of the Niagara Falls district and taxation on the Canadian side. They were able to show me why their meals on the Canadian side cost between 20 per cent and 30 per cent more than comparable meals on the American side. It is this type of thing which is causing tourism to fall off. I feel the $8 extension of the airport tax will only heighten this trend.
To those who have read the budgetary papers, it must be apparent that the average Canadian pays substantially more in the form of sales tax, excise tax and what-have-you than does the average American. In the discussion paper which was issued with the June 23 budget of 1975 there is a table showing the relative position with regard to taxes on goods and services in the United States and Canada. Table 3 at page 14 of the discussion paper which lists the incidence of these taxes in the two countries rates Canada in 1972, for example, as having a level of 25.2 per cent. The level in the United States in the same year was 16.2 per cent. This shows, to the extent that the sales tax and the excise tax are regressive, to the extent that they hit the poor person as opposed to the person with relatively higher income, that our tax system is considerably more regressive than that of the United States. The difference is that 16.2 per cent of the revenue of the United States comes from this form of taxation, whereas in Canada it is 25.2 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, sound taxation policies can accomplish two distinct aims. On the one hand, the imposition of a tax can inhibit or control activity. On the other, the removal of taxes can encourage a desired activity. Both of these factors come

May 20, 1977
Excise Tax
into play with the air transportation tax. Unfortunately, this government has always been too quick to deter and regulate activity through new taxes, while it is slow to encourage positive action through the removal of old taxes. This is true, of course, with the air tax, and it also true of the sales and excise tax on automobiles. Here, again, the government seems to be 180 degrees off base.
The government, we were told in the last debate on excise tax, has initiated a weight tax and levy on air conditioners as a measure to encourage energy efficient vehicles. However, when we checked, we found that weight alone is not a concise measurement of energy usage as some models, though heavier, get better fuel economy than other lighter, but more wasteful models. The weight tax, as it is set up, would not accomplish its stated aim-to reduce energy consumption-but, rather, would only serve to add yet another source of revenue to the growing excise receipts. These receipts totalled, last year, some $5 billion if customs duty and excise and sales taxes are taken together.
We urged the government to change its tax criteria to fall in line with fuel efficiency rather than mere weight. We also suggested that the sales tax on lighter cars be dropped both as a spur to the economy and as a real incentive for the purchase of energy conscious vehicles. To date, of course, nothing has happened with either of these proposals and the government has once again chosen to pass up an opportunity for positive action in favor of the more regressive use of taxation. The 12 per cent sales tax on automobiles strikes hardest at those least able to afford it. Its removal would give a tax break to those most likely to benefit from it while providing a more direct approach to this nation's energy goals. I repeat, not only would it be in the interest of energy conservation but it would be a spur to employment in this country in that our automotive industry is oriented toward the production of smaller cars, more efficient cars, rather than to the heavier models.
We look forward to discussing this matter again with the minister when this bill moves into committee of the whole. On average today, Canadian automobiles cost between $500 and $1,000 more than their American counterparts. The lion's share of the difference lies in the taxes, and the taxes piled on taxes, extracted by governments. It is worth while to note, for example, that the Americans dropped their excise tax on automobiles in 1971 in order to stimulate the economy. They did this despite the fact that in some states-Michigan, for example-the revenue from the excise tax was greater than that produced by income taxes.
The average sales tax on Canadian automobiles is probably the largest single factor contributing to the higher cost of cars here. It is Ottawa which is the largest beneficiary of the production of automobiles. By this, I mean that if you break down the cost of an automobile, you find it is Ottawa which makes more money with respect to its purchase than anybody else: more than the car manufacturer, be it Ford or General Motors; more than the wholesaler; more than the dealer; more than any provincial government. In short, it makes between $300 and $1,000 on the purchase of every automobile in this

country, and then has the nerve to say it would like, somehow, to discourage inflation. Well, Mr. Speaker, one way in which the government could get less inflation is by reducing the excise tax on smaller cars, making them cheaper for the average man who needs them to commute to work.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At one o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. When the House rose at one o'clock, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) had the floor on Bill C-54.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Before the lunch break I was indicating that we felt consideration should be given by the minister to the elimination or reduction of the federal sales tax on energy-efficient cars. I was pointing out that perhaps the largest single factor contributing to the higher cost of cars in Canada compared with the United States is that Ottawa maintains its excise tax, the United States tax having been removed in 1971. To put the matter in perspective, let me take, for example, a $3,200, four-cylinder Chevette. How many of us realize that the manufacturer makes about $75 on that car, the retailer makes about $100, yet the net take in sales tax alone which accrues to the federal government is $320. In other words, 10 per cent of the final retail price of that automobile actually goes to the federal government.
I suggest that that is not only inflationary in the sense that it causes people to pay that additional amount for a car, but it puts a hardship on the very people who should get relief in this country, namely, the average working person who needs a car to commute to work. Thirdly, it is a disincentive to people to buy a relatively small car, not only the Chevette to which I have referred but other similar types of automobiles.
Another item we will take up in committee of the whole is the excise tax on gasoline. Originally, the government declared that another gasoline tax amounting to 10 cents a gallon was necessary to support oil prices in Canada below the international market price. This tax was to be used, and has been used, to finance compensation payments to offset the cost of imported oil. As has been noted in the House, the 10 cents a gallon excise tax and the export tax levy currently produce revenue which exceeds the compensation payments by something like $300 million. As the domestic price of oil reaches the international market level, the need for this tax disappears, yet the revenues produced by it will increase. Here again, this windfall profit appears to be dropping into the hands of a government which, from its past record, has been irresponsible in the handling of such funds, certainly so far as their own restraint in expenditure is concerned.
In closing, let me add that we on this side of the House welcome the sales tax exemption for businesses with an annual
May 20, 1977

turnover of S10,000 or less. These will now be exempt from the sales tax provisions. This is something for which we on this side of the House have been asking for some time and we are pleased that the government has at last acceded to this request on our part. Incidentally, this provision removes an important obstacle to the small, independent Canadian craftsman and is long overdue.
Your Honour will recall that in the budget address of March 31, when dealing with other tax changes the minister stated:
Finally, I want to refer to the discussion paper on federal sales and excise taxation. The issue here is whether the tax should be shifted from the manufacturer's level to the wholesale level. The matter requires further consideration. The report of the commodity tax review group will be tabled shortly in the House. I have asked the President of the Privy Council to refer the report to an appropriate standing committee of the House for its assessment.
I am pleased that the minister has not forgotten that discussion paper and that he intends to table it shortly. This will enable us to have a debate and to review the matter in the House. I am not pleased with the fact that there seems to be prolonged study, study and study, with so little activity. As we review the discussion paper and subsequent comments concerning the possibility of having the sales tax changed from the manufacturing level to the wholesale level, there seems to be almost a predetermined government decision. If we refer to the discussion paper the minister referred to in his March 31 budget, we find stated under item 11 on page 7: "Consequently the government proposes to move the application of the federal sales tax from the manufacturers' level to the wholesale level." They have said that and they propose to do it.
[DOT] (UlO)
The minister made a very brief comment in his budget speech concerning the possibility of a wholesale tax. In the budget document there are almost two pages dealing with commodity taxes. We also find that while the government admits they have received 200 major submissions with respect to their proposals to change the sales tax from the manufacturers' level to the wholesale level, they go through the pros and the cons. They seem to end up in the budget document back to the point where they were in 1975, stating that most of the objections are admitted. They think it was a good idea, in spite of the objections. Surely it is a rather strange thing to have discussion papers issued, invite submissions, acknowledge objections and then turn around and say that in any event it should be put into effect.
If we reach committee of the whole before four o'clock, I hope the minister will make some comments later today. We may accept this coming into the House for further debate, but surely now is the time the minister should be bringing us up to date as to what his current thinking is on this important subject. I know certain of my colleagues wish to speak on this bill. I will conclude, but I do intend to ask questions at the committee of the whole stage on this important bill.

Mr. Speaker, it was less than four months ago that I rose to debate a bill to amend the Excise Tax Act. That was not Bill C-54; it was Bill C-21.
Excise Tax
It is interesting to note there has been no change in principle in the amendments which are proposed by this bill. Four months ago, in January, I was complaining about the nature of this tax. I said then, and I would like to say again, that it is an unfair kind of tax because the people in Canada who are paying the tax are not properly informed of it.
Unless one has particular knowledge of law, or particular knowledge of business, one does not have this tax brought to his attention and yet he carries on paying it all the time. Taxes are necessary. Everyone knows that. But it is the duty of the government to be honest and tell people when they are levying a tax and to clearly let them know a tax is being levied. A further inequitable part of this tax is that it, itself, is taxed by nine out of the ten provinces in Canada. Thus, this tax is increased by the percentage charged in retail sales taxes by those provinces.
We have heard a lot of talk about equity and simplicity in tax systems. That should not be only applied to income taxes. There is no reason why it could not apply to this tax. The constant changes the government feels compelled to introduce continually illustrate there is no equity and no simplicity in this tax as well as many others.
I would like to refer to the minister's budget speech at page 16 where he made reference to the discussion paper on federal sales and excise taxation. That paper was introduced by the former minister of finance, Mr. Turner, in June of 1975, approximately two years ago. The present minister, in his budget speech on March 31, 1977, said that the issue is whether the tax should be shifted from the manufacturers' level to the wholesale level and that the matter requires further consideration. At the time that discussion paper was issued there were thousands of representations made from all across Canada about whether the system should be changed to shift the burden from the manufacturers' level to the wholesale level, or not.
With the lapse of two years, with these thousands of submissions which have been received by the government, the government should have been able to come up with some kind of policy. The minister said that the matter requires further study and he went on to say that the report of the commodity tax review group will be tabled shortly in the House. We know what "shortly" means in this House: it means we will be lucky to see it this fall. In his budget speech he went on to say:
I have asked the President of the Privy Council to refer the report to an appropriate standing committee of the House for its assessment.
That is another delay, Mr. Speaker. A standing committee on something like that is going to take further prolonged time. Goodness knows when we will ever see the results of the discussion paper on federal sales and excise taxation. I suspect it is a change that is not really wanted.
I should like to look at some of the provisions of the bill now before us. I notice the minister proposes to make some changes to sales tax exemptions for small manufacturers. He is going to increase that exemption from $3,000 to $10,000. Knowing the last time that exemption was changed, I am quite sure the increase to $10,000 does no more than keep up with the rate of

May 20, 1977
Excise Tax
inflation on manufactured goods. The complaint has been made often enough that the minister should be aware of it by now. This is a tax which is also applied to offices which do a little in-house printing with copying machines, or whatever, if they are above the exemption.
Even the small individual businesses in manufacturing cannot get by without manufacturing more than $10,000 a year worth of goods. When they exceed that and have to start paying the excise tax, in addition to all the rest of their taxes, they have a very difficult time indeed. Further consideration is still warranted on that provision. It is commendable that certain producers of craft products, which are significant to Canadian culture and heritage, are going to be helped out, too, although that does not seem to be spelled out too well.
We can commend the fact that some additional energy-conserving items will be excepted. I notice there has been no specific reference by the goverment to help recycling industries. One or two of them will come in under this exemption because recycled newsprint is now being used in the manufacture of insulation. That will be considered as an energy-conserving item. Other items were mentioned in the supplementary budget papers. I am referring to page 25, aides to the disabled. The minister is certainly to be commended for extending the exemption to wheelchair lifts and allowing power to the governor in council to prescribe by regulation. Although we on this side have often said that government by regulation is bad and should not be encouraged, in the circumstances we can at least say that the motive is good.
With regard to the exemption being extended to vehicles which are designed to carry 12 or more passengers, the minister should again be commended-and I do not like doing that too much, in having discovered a loophole whereby some of these vehicles were being used as individual, private recreation vehicles. That certainly was not the intent. I submit that if the government had been doing its job properly in the first place, the present correction would not be necessary.
The minister said that the aim of the air transport tax is that an equitable contribution will be made toward the upkeep of facilities. More work is needed in this area as abuses are still possible. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) mentioned the problem of airport funding, in particular where some of this money was going to go and the hardship this tax would impose on the tourist business. It is possible to circumvent this $8 ticket tax by simply buying a single ticket which covers, say, six return trips.
Every couple of weeks or so I fly to my constituency. I pay an $8 tax on a return ticket. However, the system in no way prevents me from buying a single ticket for six return trips and paying only one $8 tax. The minister will probably suggest that there are very few people who will do that. His predecessor said that to me on many occasions, for example, with regard to the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. However, whether there are numerous people who will do certain things or not is not the point. The point is that the
(Mr. Clarke.]
government should make its regulations to ensure that they are equitable and applied equally.
This ties in with another abuse that is open-the matter of stopovers. When you buy a ticket and travel from one place to another in Canada, you may stop over as many times as you wish. You will only pay one $8 airport tax. The minister says it is for the upkeep of the facilities in the airports. The stopover passenger uses the facilities just as much as a passenger coming from outside the country, or any other passenger. The use is equal in all cases, but the demand is not. It would be a very simple matter for the government to correct this situation.
I will give an example. The airlines, including the government-owned Air Canada, charge sector fares when there are stopovers during a longer trip. Even though they are able to increase their revenue by charging sector fares, the government has ignored the possibility of collecting this extra tax which the minister says they need in order that travellers who use the facilities pay for them on an equal basis.
Many of my colleagues have commented on the gasoline tax. I will make only one or two comments. I understand that it is to be adjusted, but I am not clear on the purpose of the adjustment. This is a good time to ask ourselves why the government continues to levy the ten-cent per gallon tax which penalizes Canadians who must drive. I am not referring to those who are entitled to a refund, but those who must drive and do not get a refund. Considering the size of Canada, the lack of public transit and the fact that the government allows the price of oil to rise toward world levels, those who need to move about for business and other purposes are penalized by this tax.
Comment has been made on the concessions for smaller cars. The hon. member for York-Simcoe referred to the contrast in prices of automobiles between Canada and the United States and how the content of prices in Canada is largely made up of the extra sales tax that Canadians must pay.
Although it has been suggested a number of times, the government has not yet given any consideration to concessions with regard to the length of time a vehicle might last. The considerations of the government are strictly with regard to fuel economy. While one cannot argue with that, we should keep in mind the energy consumption required for the production of motor vehicles. Consideration should be given to encouraging Canadians to make their cars last longer.
One place where it could make a start would be in the capital city of Canada, right here in Ottawa. We have a very expensive commission-the National Capital Commission- that seems to be in control of things in Ottawa. Enormous amounts of salt are put on the streets in winter. It is not as though this were the only place in Canada that has a lot of snow. Many places on the prairies have a lot of snow and cold weather, but they get along without extensive use of salt. Obviously, the automobiles last a lot longer. In my city of Vancouver, the use of salt is almost unheard of. Cars last a very long time.
May 20, 1977

I wish to make some final comments on the remarks of the hon. member for York-Simcoe. He stated that this is a regressive tax, that further exemptions are needed to give relief to low-income Canadians. I certainly support that. I have called for this before. There should be exemptions for all food, housing costs, clothing and other necessities. It is clear that a wheelchair, which is exempt, is no more of a necessity to a crippled person than the other basic needs of a society.
While 1 find much to agree with in this bill, I think the government has again failed to give the needed deep consideration to the major changes of principle that are needed in the application of this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to follow the lead of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in his complaints about the application of the airport tax as it is being handled by the Ministry of Transport. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is not with us this afternoon. Perhaps the message will get through to him, although I have to admit it is difficult to get any kind of message across to that minister.
I feel that I have a grievance, along with several thousand other people who are required to use the terminal facilities at Toronto international airport. People seem to be getting used to terminal 2 which is there. It was a badly designed and misconceived building. Nevertheless, it is there. In order to make the whole complex a little more workable, several million dollars were spent to connect terminal 1 with terminal 2 by means of an underground tunnel.
This would be a useful thing if it could be used, but I find that it is difficult to use unless you happen to be travelling without any form of luggage, because if you check your luggage through in order to get a reasonable connection, you cannot expect to find your luggage when you arrive at your destination beyond Toronto. If a reasonable arrangement could be worked out for the use of that tunnel, whereby a person could carry his luggage with him through it, then we might be getting something for this added excise tax on travel.
It is bad enough to have to wait for the luggage to come off, but what makes it impossible is the fact that people have to run upstairs and wait for that little bus to carry them across to terminal two with their suitcases. 1 think that machine comes around about every 15 minutes, and if a person misses it, as is normal, he has to wait half an hour. By that time it is too late to catch the connection over to the other terminal. We have a facility which cost several million dollars, and it has not been useful on any occasion on which I have used it. When I have left my luggage behind, I have found nobody in the facility, and it has been something like a mausoleum.
It is high time the government became a little more efficient with the taxes it handles, and in this connection we are dealing with amendments to tax legislation which raise about 25 per cent of the total revenue of the government. Many taxes are hidden and people do not realize they are actually paying
Excise Tax
them. Nevertheless, they do account for a tremendous source of revenue for the government. The government should account for the way it handles that money because at the present time it is just not handling it properly.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) and the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) mentioned the discussion paper which was issued by the previous minister of finance two years ago. I wish some headway could be made in this area. Speaking for myself, I am little discouraged to find that the government and its advisers are moving toward shifting taxation from the manufacturing level to the wholesale level. As a matter of principle, I think the government should be more accountable for its taxation policies. I think there should be a shift to the retail sales level. If that were done, the amount the government is taking would be out in the open. If we keep it at the manufacturing or the wholesale level, it is a hidden tax and in many cases adds to the apparent cost of everything. Retailers generally fix their mark-up on the basis of the wholesale cost, and then take a percentage on the amount of sales and excise tax they have to pay to the federal government.
This may not be a politically easy move to make, but I think an effort to make governments more accountable is necessary. It should be harder for governments to raise money and this source of revenue should be moved out into the open. Then there would be more accountability on the part of the government.
I agree with what my hon. friends have said about delay. An improvement should certainly be made in the form of taxation, and I urge this government to move past the wholesale level to the retail level. This would probably be fairly difficult in the province of Alberta, a part of which I represent. At the present time in Alberta there is no direct sales tax. My proposal would mean the imposition of a sales tax, and if I were on the government side I probably would not want this. However, as a matter of principle, these things should be out in the open.
I join in congratulating the Department of Finance for increasing the exemption with regard to small manufacturers. I believe this measure is aimed toward benefiting people involved in voluntary social activities. I believe it is unfortunate that the government has got into so many areas of social welfare. People are beginning to expect everything to be done by the government in that area and volunteer activities are falling by the wayside. That is much to the detriment of the basic nature and fabric of our society. This is a small step to encourage voluntary movements, and I hope the government will not let it lie here but that it will take other steps to encourage people to help themselves and others through voluntary activities, rather than having massive government programs to solve everybody's problems-which the government has not been very adept in doing, in any event.
I wanted to make another point with regard to the Toronto airport and the cost of living. The fare for that little bus to which I referred used to be 10 cents. It took people from one terminal to another. Now it costs 25 cents. That is quite an increase, percentagewise; and there is no fee at all for the use

May 20, 1977
Excise Tax
of that multi-million dollar tunnel. It seems strange to me that we cannot better utilize facilities which have already been installed and, therefore, make us a little more efficient.
In Vancouver, the bus is free.

It will not be for long, if we have the Minister of Transport and his user-pay concept around here much longer.
I would like also to comment on the business of car taxes. I am astounded that this government persists, in this area of high taxation, to increase those taxes. I can see some point in using taxation to encourage the use of energy-efficient automobiles, but the government's approach seems to be to increase taxes on large cars, which are already too high, and to leave the tax on smaller cars at the same level. I would rather see the government do something to reduce its total taxation "take" by removing, or reducing, taxes on energy-efficient models; and if a tax must remain on the other ones, they should be left at their present level.
Reference has also been made to the excise tax on gasoline. I agree with the government's state policy of increasing the price of petroleum to world levels, but the government should practice what it preaches and reduce the excise tax in the same proportion as applies to the price of oil, from which gasoline is extracted, because the stated objective is to reduce imports, and as that gap narrows the stated reason for the tax narrows. The government has an obligation to the people of Canada to refuse a tax that no longer has a reason for being.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the government is asking us to amend legislation that accounts for a major source of its income. Numerous examples have been given to indicate they are not using this income properly. Because of that, I feel, as a general principle, they should be made more accountable and the public should be made more aware of this type of taxation. It should be out in the open. This would force the government to be more efficient with the money they take from taxpayers in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take just a few minutes of the time of the House to present to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) an appeal which I readily admit has been made to me by only two persons. I suspect, however, that their view represents that of many others, and I hope the minister will give it consideration or at least ask some of his experts to look at it. The two persons who wrote me in this vein are from different parts of the country and I see no reason to think they were acting in concert. In each case the person is about to become an old age pensioner and retire. To use the language in one of the letters, this man and his wife have looked forward to their retirement for a long time.
We look forward to yours.

My hon. friend says that he and some of his friends are looking forward to my retirement. They will have to look forward to it from somewhere else, because they will be gone from this place long before I am.
This man and his wife had planned their retirement for a long time, he writes, and would like to see Canada. They have a car and a small trailer and had planned to make a trip and see Canada in the first year of their retirement. But he says that the tremendous increase in the price of gasoline has just about put that plan out of the picture.
The argument he makes to me is that he did not know 5, 10 or 20 years ago what was going to happen. Surely some concession might be made to such persons. I am not standing here making an appeal that all persons aged 65 and over should not have to pay the gasoline excise tax. After all, that would include me-and I am in a position to pay it, being a member of parliament. I put it to the minister, however, that as there are already some exceptions-farmers, certain invalids, and so on-in terms of the excise tax on gasoline, I wonder if a way could not be found to assist senior citizens, especially those who are not employed, who do not have other income and who might have to meet any other conditions the minister or his officials would work out. I am not trying to give the details. I am honoured that there are eight or ten of the minister's top officials in the gallery, so I am sure they could work out the details.
As I said, this appeal has been made to me by only two persons but I make no apology for taking the time of the House in regard to it. It is a reasonable, human appeal and I hope the minister and his officials will take a good look at it.

Mr. Speaker, 1 will take this opportunity to offer a few comments and express a few concerns I have about the air transport tax proposed in Bill C-54. There are some conflicts in what is happening in Canada today that bring me to my feet to offer these remarks. Canada is at a low ebb in its economy and its ability to employ its people, but here we are moving in with another obstacle toward creating some energy within the travel market in the country. This air transport tax is a double taxation when considered with the tax in the United States. If you purchase a ticket in New York to go to Montreal and return, you are subject to a S3 U.S. tax-which, by the way, is sent into a trust fund that the federal aviation authority operates for expenditures on airways and airports. Then you have to pay another $8 tax to Canada.
The Canadian tax apparently goes to the administration of air transportation or the airport revolving fund, which in 1976 received $29.7 million in air transport tax-a substantial increase over the $5.7 million received in 1975. It is not practical to collect this tax at the other end.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and his staff are aware how the system works in Europe. There, half of all tickets are sold by interline airlines, one-quarter by travel agents and one-quarter by the carrying airlines. How could the
May 20, 1977

collection of this tax be co-ordinated in a market like Europe when we are trying to attract some of their tourist dollars to this country? What we seem to be doing is imposing bad attitudes on tourists; on the one hand we welcome them, and on the other hand we send them off with a scowl.
In order to collect this $8 tax from foreign tourists we will have to accost them as they leave Canada and it will have to be done by the airline. In the United States, if a visitor refuses to pay his $3 tax the airline has the passenger sign a slip which the airline turns over to the government, which then has the responsibility of collecting. Where the tax is only S3, it is unlikely that the government will try to collect it.
Let us take the case of a family of four departing from Montreal. First, there is the bus ride from downtown to the airport-four times $5, making $20. If the airport tax was not collected at the European end of the trip-which is most unlikely-it has to be collected by the clerk at the airline counter. So four times $8 is $32. What a farewell for a family that has come to enjoy Canada. Of course, they could refuse to pay, which would give rise to all kinds of problems. It would hold up business at the counter and queues would lengthen.
Then there is the problem of handling the cash involved in this transaction. Most tickets are prepaid or purchased by credit card, so the visitor might have to join another queue in order to pay this tax that the airline is asked to collect on behalf of the government. What a way to build a travel industry! Why do we risk people leaving the country with a sour attitude?
It was suggested that the tax be collected through the customs and excise officials at the airport, but they pointed out that it would involve them in union problems. What will happen with the airlines if they are landed with this problem on top of their already onerous duties? I say this because, at this time in our history airlines can only cut costs and balance revenues with expenditures by cutting down on personnel. I suggest we are applying unnecessary pressure.
Consider what would happen to a person visiting Canada who bought his ticket in Europe. Since the carrier has brought the passenger only one way, from Europe to this country, the contract of carriage has only been half fulfilled. Let us suppose that the passenger will not pay the tax. What could happen? The airline could choose to break the contract of carriage, could choose not to collect the tax and be liable to penalties under the act and, perhaps, in the process, be responsible for that passenger missing his departure flight. The airline would then face the prospect of paying for the overnight accommodation. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, this position would add burdens to the industry already severely burdened with problems.
Largely because we insist on passing measures like Bill C-58, other countries are retaliating against us. The United States government will not allow U.S. citizens attending conventions in Canada to deduct their convention expenses for purposes of income tax. So in the United Kingdom there has
Excise Tax
arisen the question of retaliation with respect to security costs against Canadian airlines, because United Kingdom airlines are forced to pay security charges in Canada, whereas such services are provided in England by the British equivalent to our Department of Transport. This kind of retaliation is starting to build up against us-and we do not need it, especially at this time.
No doubt the government will claim that the collection of the transport tax in other countries is a step in the right direction. They say it is an equitable step, for, if Canadians must pay, why should not others? I suggest that if we welcome others to this country we should not involve them in the sort of hassles which could be in prospect for them. Really, this awkward tax which could create unnecessary problems would not have been necessary if the government had paid more attention to the management of the revolving fund set up to finance the construction of airports and airport facilities. I suggest the Taj Mahal syndrome, to quote the Minister of Transport, has made this tax, or this source of revenue, necessary.
In 1969 we set up the revolving fund for operating the two eastern airports. Then the Vancouver airport was included. According to what I learned in the public accounts committee, the revolving fund seemed to be working well and was actually generating a surplus. What happens under this government? The revolving fund was working well, apparently, the idea underlying it conforming to the user-pay policy of the Minister of Transport, when, without warning, the government absolutely ruined it, decimated it. It used the revolving fund as the burying ground for a whole series of unnecessary costs. First, it buried the some $500 million cost of Mirabel in that revolving fund. These days, when you ask how much Mirabel cost, it is difficult to obtain a truthful answer. The government will not say how much Mirabel cost it.
It doesn't know.

It does not know, and there is no way for it to find out. The government has used DREE for these purposes, the airport revolving fund, the Department of Public Works-it has used every little basket, so to speak, available to it to hide the cost of that airport. As well, the cost of the bridge from Vancouver to Sea Island has been hidden in that revolving fund. The government put the $130 million for the Calgary airport under the revolving fund, as well as the Pickering land purchase. Mr. Speaker, by so doing it is destroying the user-pay concept. By so using this revolving fund, that concept will be shattered. The government has really turned the fund into a coffin for its extravagance.
I have been a principal supporter of the user-pay policy which was put forward by the previous minister of transport and continued by the present occupant of that portfolio. But as I note the waste and extravagance of the government, and the unnecessary burden it is forcing our revenue-generators to bear, I cannot continue to support the user-pay concept. Our revenues in this regard should be solidly based, and sound. I think the opportunity to persuade people to accept the user-

May 20, 1977
Excise Tax
pay concept in this country has been destroyed by this kind of abuse of government structures.
I have not much more to say, except that this tax is being rammed through the House without justification. The Minister of Transport and his staff are aware of the points I have made, but they are not listening to the industry. You would think that the minister, after his experience in withdrawing the northland subsidy on the west coast, would stop persisting in being arrogant and begin listening to suggestions which could have a positive effect in Canada. To me, this airport user-pay tax is contrary to the spirit of the user-pay policy the government has tried to promote in this country.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to bring to the attention of the minister a problem not new to him, since the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) drew it to his attention about a month ago. The question relates to the excise tax on potting soils and mixtures which has suddenly been resurrected. The question was brought to my attention by a constituent, Hillview Farms Limited, who 10 or 12 years ago realized there was a market in Canada for potting soil and potting soil mixtures. The company had to choose between two types of product, a mixture of various inert materials which, by themselves, could not support vegetable life, or a mixture composed partly of soil and partly of inert materials.
It learned from federal authorities that if it used a mixture of soil and inert materials it would not need to pay the manufacturer's sales tax, but if it mixed a number of these inert materials mechanically, in an admixture, sales tax could be charged. On the basis of that information the company consulted an agricultural expert who said that if the company wished to do a service to the Canadian horticultural industry it would opt for the second alternative, a mixture of true soil and certain inert ingredients which would foster the growth of plants. Having the best interests of the consumer and the country at heart, that company started a small operation in which it employed one or two people part-time. It has now grown, employing some 18 or 20 people full-time, and extra help in the summer.
Lo and behold, they were informed this winter, about two or three months ago, by the income tax officials that the income tax people had apparently just woken up from some kind of lethargy or sleep and had just discovered that some ten or twelve years ago legislation had been provided under the Excise Tax Act which called for a manufacturing sales tax on these products. This was news to them, of course, because they had been advised otherwise, and they consulted us about it. We, in turn, informed the Minister of National Revenue. The hon. lady took the matter under consideration and decided that something should be done about it. No concessions could be allowed in this area and I was so informed by her.
At the same time, the minister brought the matter to the attention of her colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), who I see is in his place today. We are pleased he is here and are interested to note that he has at least a dozen
of his experts sitting in the gallery. I am sure the hon. gentleman will be able to give us an answer later today or next week, because from such a large batch of experts I am sure he will be able to obtain a good explanation of this problem.
One wonders why the income tax people suddenly found this section of the act when it had been completely ignored for so many years. One wonders whether it was a case that somebody just woke up and realized it was there. On the other hand, it may constitute evidence that there is in Canada a fairly large corporation, a subsidiary of an American corporation, which happens to import into Canada these inert products which are then sold on the market. Because they do not contain any soil they therefore, in accordance with the act, incur tax, and this is as it should be. If this is the case, they may be having difficulty competing with our own Canadian companies which produce a superior product. Perhaps the minister can confirm that pressure has been brought to bear, if not on his department then certainly on the Department of National Revenue, with a view to taxing this particular product, which is now available in Canada, in order to give a better chance to the American corporation with its Canadian subsidiary.
One wonders on what basis the Minister of Finance determines when a tax will apply on products such as soils and soil mixtures. It appears to have something to do with the term "manufacture". I have experienced difficulty in finding out what the ministry means when referring to manufacturing as it applies to soil mixtures and potting soils. These mixtures are nothing but mechanical mixtures. Soil is put with some of these inert materials and they are mixed together. No chemical reaction takes place. Any of the products used in the mixture remains unchanged, and yet for some reason the interpretation placed on the product by the Department of Finance is that the material has undergone a manufacturing process. On the other hand, if ordinary soil is taken and is treated with radiation or some other treatment which changes the soil, removes the bacteria from the soil, or may change it in some other way from its original condition, we then find that no tax applies. It is not considered, in that case, to be manufacturing. Therefore it is very difficult to know precisely what definition is used to arrive at the term "manufacturing".
A fundamental premise also exists, I understand, in the philosophy of the Department of Finance when they are trying to categorise products such as this. If you have a naturally occurring product in bulk and package it for use by the consumer in a smaller, more acceptable form, tax is not incurred. This makes sense, and when ordinary soil is packaged in this way no tax is incurred. But try to do the same with a bulk quantity of soil and add a few inert materials to it. For some strange reason tax is incurred when this mixture is repackaged.
This is not a minor matter, Mr. Speaker.
