It is one of major significance to many firms across Canada because it is my understanding that not only is Hillview Farms Ltd. concerned about it but that increasing concern is being expressed by the industry as a whole. Organizations such as Flowers Canada, Landscape Ontario, and Landscape Canada are most con-

May 20, 1977

cerned about this sudden imposition or re-incarnation of a tax which has been on the books for years but which had never been implemented. This may signify the efficiency of the government when it has taxes on the books for years but fails to implement them.
There are a number of inconsistencies, anomalies, inequities, and absurdities which relate to this problem, one which itself is something of an absurdity. First of all, it is interesting to note that these materials which are now about to be taxed in Canada can be imported tax free from, say, the United States if they come in containers with a plant or a flower in them. It is an odd situation. One can deduce that a person in Canada who needs potting soil has only to import it from the United States in containers.
There is a second inequity here. We are, in fact, faced with a hidden tax on food. I do not think the Minister of Finance really believes food should be taxed. But this is the situation. If you want to grow some tomatoes yourself, or if you want to grow some cabbage plants or some cauliflower plants, anything like that, for food for yourself you will be obliged, from now on, to pay a tax on the potting soil mixture you will need. It will be an added cost to be considered by all who grow food for themselves.
A third point which should be mentioned concerns discrimination. As we debate this tax bill, meetings are going on in one of our standing committees in relation to discrimination in relation to human rights legislation. Here we have a government which is trying to get away from discrimination in the field of human rights now reintroducing discrimination in another form. In Canada at the present time we have roughly 250 companies manufacturing potting soils of one kind or another. To the best of my knowledge, of those 250 companies the income tax officials have decided to nail only three of them. This is discrimination. They have said, in effect, that these three companies, presumably because they are a little more successful than the others, will be the guinea pigs and will have this reincarnated tax tried out on them. Instead of being fair to all the industries and agencies manufacturing potting soils or soil mixtures, we find the tax department has picked on three and is demanding the tax from them.
To illustrate how ridiculous the situation is and to show how inconsiderate the government is being in the way it has handled this matter, we will, for the sake of argument, concede that the tax is a proper one. We do not believe it is, of course, but let us just concede that for the moment. We have a situation where, in January or February of the year, in midwinter, the income tax people challenge the manufacturer of potting soils and say, "Starting now, you must pay 12 per cent manufacturing sales tax." They do not seem to realize the problems faced by these manufacturers. They do not seem to recognize that they issue catalogues, and plan for months in advance. All their prices are already catalogued, their invoicing and billing are done by computerized systems, and it takes at least three months to change them and costs about $8,000. Some of these companies deliver their soil well in advance, and often do not require payment until many months later. There
Excise Tax
are many complications, all of which the Department of Revenue has decided to ignore.
One further anomaly which I did touch on earlier refers to the fact that you can take ordinary soil and sterilize it, or subject it to radiation, but that does not seem to incur any tax; that does not seem to be interpreted as manufacturing. Take, for example, medical equipment. That is prepackaged, like soil, and does not incur any tax. But if you take ordinary soil and put a little bit of peat moss or vermiculite or fertilizer or other ingredient into it, you end up with what is called a manufactured product, and for some reason you then have to pay tax.
There is also what is known as spent soil. Nurserymen, market gardeners, and mushroom growers use a type of soil which, after a certain amount of use, becomes known as spent soil. For some reason spent soils are not taxable. I have before me a letter from the Minister of National Revenue under date of April, 1977, in reply to a question I put to her, and she has this to say in regard to soils:
Soils in their natural state are not taxable, even when packaged. In the same vein, spent or surplus soils sold by nurserymen, market gardeners, and mushroom producers are also not taxable. These soils have not been processed nor have new characteristics or qualities been added to them prior to their sale-at least to the extent that they could be regarded as being manufactured or produced.
There seems to be something of a caveat there, but who would believe, Mr. Speaker, that a nurseryman, a mushroom grower or market gardener using these special soils had not added something to them? They may have added fertilizer or peat moss or vermiculite, yet according to the way the minister interprets the Excise Tax Act this soil is not manufactured. If a constituent of mine takes the natural products and puts them together, for some reason the end product is called manufactured. I do not know how the minister can explain that anomaly but possibly we will hear from him on the matter later today or sometime next week.
Having described these half dozen anomalies in the interpretation of the Excise Tax Act I should like, in conclusion, to put three questions to the minister to see whether I can bring the matter to a head and obtain some explanation from him. First of all, I presume it will not be the responsibility of the minister, but someone will have to monitor this beastly tax which has been uncovered. It is pretty difficult to decide just what is in soil, dirt. If there is vermiculite or perlite in it, that will be easy to identify, but I challenge anyone to say that soil with a little bit of peat moss or fertilizer or manure in it is different from soil you get out of the ground which has not been so-called manufactured, as the minister says it is.
In other words, how is the minister going to tell when soil has actually been mechanically mixed by some process compared with when it has been taken from the ground and bagged and is thus not taxable? I think the minister, or perhaps his colleague, has opened up a real bag of worms here, which is an appropriate metaphor. I suggest the department will have difficulty deciding whether a given soil mixture was

May 20, 1977
Excise Tax
taken naturally from the ground or mixed together by some mechanical means.
Secondly, supposing a manufacturer of these soil mixtures, instead of combining them together as they are currently in a manner which is helpful to the consumer-obviously this service has been popular in view of the growth from two employees to 20-decides to package each ingredient in his soil mixtures separately so as not to incur tax, or puts all these little packages into one big package, presumably it still would not incur tax. 1 suggest it is ludicrous to think a manufacturer would have to do that in order to avoid this rather absurd and inane tax.
My final question to the minister is this: would he study the question of potting soil and potting soil mixtures from the point of view of all the inequities and anomalies to which I have referred? A very small amount of money is going to be raised from this resurrected tax and difficulty will be caused many businesses in Canada, and undeservedly so. I ask the minister to give consideration to including a clause in the bill to exempt from sales tax potting soil mixtures, top soil, top dressings and other similar products.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to enter the debate on excise taxation. It strikes me that the Departments of Revenue and Finance are still a little too imbued with some of the philosophy which appeared in the Carter commission report some years ago. There is a little too much tendency to say a buck is a buck is a buck, and for the federal government to demand money by way of taxation, as the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) suggested was the case with the airline tax, rather than look at ways in which to restrict federal spending, in which case the need to be quite so rapacious in taxation would not be there.
I also hope that in the next budget there will be a thoroughgoing review of federal excise tax, which has been promised us. I hope it will include a move to make the federal share of sales tax a visible, open tax, which the public could recognize each time it makes a purchase. I realize that the Constitution is clear on this point and that the federal government has the right to impose a hidden tax, whereas the provincial governments have not and must, if necessary, impose visible sales taxes. Nevertheless, the practice is detrimental not only to national unity but to the economy of the country.
While this tax review is ongoing I trust that coincident with it an attempt will be made to reconcile the whole sales tax picture with the provinces. Nothing is more detrimental to national unity than varying levels of sales tax imposed, and necessarily imposed, by provincial governments across the country. This problem is particularly acute in British Columbia where the sales tax has risen to 7 per cent, with no sales tax existing in our neighbouring province. The hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) made reference to this in his speech. I know the long standing opposition of that province to the imposition of any sales tax, but the distortions which are brought into the economy of the province of British Columbia on its eastern border are so great, and the damage
[Mr. Halliday.)
to business so serious, that a conference between the national government and the provinces should be convened to try to even out sales taxes applied across the country. The federal share of it should be made visible so that the provincial government would not stand out the way it does now when the federal government can escape without the general, daily, every purpose recognition of the sales tax.
I hope the minister, in conjunction with his colleague in the Revenue Department, will instigate a thorough review of the role of the revenue office in retailing within Canada. This is particularly so when it is possible to use zenith numbers to phone, without charge, south of the border to order goods which may well be purchased at a discount price not available to a normal importer who is expected to pay the fair market price. To have those goods landed in a town in the interior of British Columbia and then hand them out on collection of the 121/2 per cent excise tax, but with no collection of the 7 per cent provincial tax, would be an automatic bargain. That may be an additional bargain in lieu of the original purchase price. The competition from the United States to small business in a province with a large provincial sales tax is very, very real. When you have a province that has two undefended borders in terms of the retailing community, it leaves a great deal of discontent amongst those people.
I suspect the Revenue Department is in many ways a long way behind the times in assessing the type and extent of excise tax which should be collected, when it seems quite possible that a manufacturer in the United States can control the wholesaler and can control the retailer and may well own the discount house as well. Thus they are able to discount their own product by dumping it abroad into Canada, which the Anti-Dumping Act does not take into consideration at the present time.
The other area I am concerned about is the area which shows up in regard to crafts. I have had a considerable amount of mail over the last year from people interested in crafts. Certainly the areas I represent in British Columbia tend to have a fairly long tradition of hand made and hand crafted articles which rise to the level of art as well. I am very much concerned about the proposed changes.
I would like to illustrate this with an example that was given to me by a constituent who creates highly original articles which are hand crafted, one of a kind, and which he calls sculpture. I notice he is not alone. 1 have here a copy of the Architectural Digest for May-June, 1977. It is the international magazine of fine interior design. I see an advertisement in that magazine for functional sculpture, signed originals by Gary Gutterman, and sold through a company called Axius in New York City. I do not know how the American excise tax department would categorize functional sculpture, but it certainly exists beyond the mind of the constituent who approached me.
An officer from the Revenue Department approached him at one of the craft shows in my constituency and informed him
May 20, 1977

that he was a manufacturer and hence not an artist. He was also informed that he should be paying the federal government sales tax on his items. He objected to that because he felt it was sculpture. Thus, an appeal was made to the customs division of the department with respect to tariff item No. 69515-1.
The Dominion customs appraiser advised my constituent that had these articles been imported they would not have been classified as sculptures under tariff item 69515-1. That misses the point a little because they were not being imported. They were being hand crafted, individually made, one of a kind, and created inside Canada, if you want to use the artistic expression. Why they should automatically fall under any definition for articles being brought in from elsewhere, I do not quite know. They are made within the country, so there is no question of duty. Why this particular suggestion was made about the treatment they would receive at the border if they had been made somewhere else, I do not know.
There is suggestion that some relief is on the way. That suggestion is contained in the statement that was made in the ways and means motion on March 31 of this year. I have the communique from Revenue Canada which sets out two provisions. It somewhat bothers me because it is ambiguous and I am sure the craft industry has not been reassured by what is here.
Before these matters are unchangeable and beyond anyone's power to revoke, I hope the minister will hold the most careful consultation with the people involved in the craft and art industry of Canada. The communique reads as follows:
The Minister of National Revenue, the Honourable Monique Begin, announced today that the regulations prescribing "Small Manufacturers" under the Excise Tax Act, will be amended to increase the annual sales value to $10,000 from the present $3,000. Persons who manufacture goods for sale or for their own use, valued at $10,000 or less annually will no longer have to be licensed or have to account for sales tax.
It continues as follows:
The minister also announced her intention to classify as small manufacturers, craftsmen who personally manufacture or produce by hand various kinds of handicrafts that reflect an aspect of Canadian culture or heritage. There will be no restriction as to annual sales volume for this group.
"Small Manufacturers" as a class are exempt from paying sales tax on the sale price of their finished products, however tax remains applicable to raw materials and components.
I suggest to the hon. minister and his hon. colleague that they will both be in endless trouble if they have two categories of small manufacturers, one being treated more generously than the other but considered a class. That makes no sense at all. It seems to me they need to change the category for small manufacturers, or they will need to introduce a third one which will deal with the artist who creates a sculpture or whatever it is which falls into the category of art. It should not be difficult to set up a board which would be able to distinguish that. It certainly would not be advisable to select the board which has approved some of the recent purchases for the National Gallery because there are some very utilitarian objects on the top floor of the gallery which have been raised to the category of art.
Excise Tax
I would suggest the Finance Minister and the Revenue Minister should have very close consultation with the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) in this regard, because their views of what constitutes art are far more stringent than the views which have been held to by the purchasing board for the National Gallery.
I suggest that the second paragraph in this category of small manufacturers-no capitals and no punctuation marks-is going to be unacceptable to the people who regard themselves as true artists or even craftsmen. To find themselves listed as a simple manufacturer does utter violence to the work in which they are engaged.
There should be some consideration of what these people are trying to do. They are trying to fulfil themselves as artists who work with the art that they have chosen as their means of expression. At the same time most of them would like to work exclusively at the art they have chosen. They do not like to be something else such as college lecturers, school teachers, service station attendants or whatever they have to be in today's inflationary society to stay afloat.
These people would like to devote their life to art. If they are lumped as manufacturers the threat will always be there that the change could very quickly be made. Given the government's need for ever-increasing sums of money, it would be very simple to change the regulations with regard to excise tax. Manufacturers would not argue the question at all as to whether it was taken off or not.
I feel that both ministries should be prepared to accept the challenge of defining what can be categorized as a living, earned, true artistic production. Whether it be pottery, sculpture or functional sculpture, there should be room for this. Otherwise these people are forced into the job market, forced to compete at a time of high unemployment, and what looks to be a period of high unemployment for some time in the future.
These people do not want to compete. They do not want to take a job that does not interest them. They do not want a job that deprives them of the opportunity of working in their chosen field. However, sheer financial necessity forces them to do that.
The $10,000 annual sales value is of utterly no help to them. If there is any question here of the amount, it should have something to do with what it costs to live in this country today, because nothing can be made from nothing. All of these people must purchase materials in order to start their creations. Their costs will continue to rise. Very likely they will have overhead costs. Fuel is needed to fire the kilns, and electricity is needed to operate the polishers.
If they sold directly, they might have a hope of making a little. However, if they have to work through a gallery or dealer and pay a percentage, the hope of the craftsman or artist receiving a large share of the $10,000 is virtually nonexistent. It is not easy to live on $10,000. If it were all profit, that would be one thing, but it is not profit. It is sales to the value of $10,000.

May 20, 1977
Excise Tax
By this measure we are forcing virtually every craftsman and artist well below the poverty line, yet taxing them on it. There is some hope in the second paragraph, but it will have to be redefined. Customs officials will be endlessly confused as to what is a small manufacturer and what is not. If a category is capital letters and quotation marks, there is not much criteria there on which they can make their decision. It will end up as in the example I quoted.
The customs officers will apply to the Revenue Department for a definition to determine what they should do with it as it crosses the border. The decision will not have anything to do with the appreciation of the craft and certainly nothing to do with the artistic merit or judgment as to the individuality of the true worth of the art as a contribution to Canada.
There is further hazard with various kinds of handicrafts being exempted if they reflect an aspect of Canadian culture or heritage. 1 am amazed to see that from this government which, for some time, has had the policy or slogan that this is a great multicultural country. Any attempt to define Canadian culture or heritage will be almost impossible. I suspect there will be a different deal for the native Indians of North America or the Inuit people than for anybody else. To define something as having a Canadian cultural or heritage aspect will be very difficult indeed.
These are my concerns about this bill. I urge the minister to have most careful consultation with his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin). There should be a thorough study of the wishes, concerns and opinions of the people involved in arts and crafts, particularly those involved in creating original objects that have to be looked at individually. There must be room for appeal for the artist who is unique, rare, and individual. In Japan, artists of that nature are classified as national treasures. However, in Canada we seem to have a policy of hoping that our artists will contribute to the national treasure, and there is a world of difference between those two approaches.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had a wide ranging debate during the day on a number of issues. Some of them ran not only beyond the bill but beyond the responsibility of this particular department, such as the questions of airport administration, the energy conservation program, and the oil import compensation program. Interesting and important as they are, I do not propose to deal with them this afternoon because, as I say, they run beyond the bill.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) raised a number of points. I appreciate his comments with regard to the increase in the small manufacturers' exemption. The point was made by him and several other members with regard to the level to which it should be raised. I should advise the House that while it has the support on one side for the notion that the level of the exemption should be increased, I and my

department have received considerable representation on the other side of the issue.
There have been objections from other small manufacturers whose volume may be above that of the groups we are talking about here. They regard it as unfair that someone who may, to a degree, be in competition, is exempt from this particular administration. That, of course, is the inevitable problem of trying to line up between what is a reasonable area of operation and what is an undue exemption in this regard. I think we can agree on the fact that at the $10,000 level we are exempting from this kind of administration a very small annual product, one which should not have to bear these costs of administration.
On the question of disability, an important and vexing question, I listened with care to what the hon. member for Edmonton West said. This matter was raised with regard to the Canada Pension Plan. It was raised in relation to the provincial administration, to which the federal government contributes through the Canada Assistance Plan. The question of disability is difficult, and disability is very painful to define with any clarity. However, I take note of the comments of the hon. member, as I took note of the comment he made with regard to marker papers for agricultural aerial sprayers. That question, perhaps, should be considered, as the hon. member mentioned, in connection with the customs tariff. I undertake that it will receive that consideration.
With regard to the air transport tax, there were a number of hon. members who made comments on the tax and on the question as to whether the imposition of this tax or a further extension of it to people who buy their tickets out of Canada and who may be engaged in a flight which causes them to deplane and to depart again from Canada, is going to operate against tourism and against the impact of more travel to Canada.
In general terms one can say that when a person is contemplating a trip by air, which is obviously going to cost several hundreds of dollars, the additional potential maximum of $8 added to the cost of that trip is obviously not going to be a disincentive. If one compares the experience with the first application of the air travel tax in 1975, after the tax was implemented in December of 1974, trans-border air travel by Canadians, which was taxable under the new tax, increased by 11.7 per cent, and other international travel by Canadians increased 9.4 per cent, so obviously questions regarding personal taste, the state of the economy, and other questions will have quite an impact on tourism, but the air tax in itself will not have that impact.
One problem which was very validly raised and which should be a matter of concern is the fact that there is a tax, for example, by the United States government on trans-border travel, and there might be an element of double taxation involved. We recognize that problem and the necessity to try to come to terms with it. Indeed, my officials have arranged
May 20, 1977

with United States officials to discuss this particular question in the very near future.
I think the problem is recognized on the United States side, and there is some hope that we might be able to achieve some kind of compromise between the two tax systems which will be of a beneficial nature.
I would like to put one other interesting statistic on the record in connection with United States visitors travelling to Canada. While there may have been a decline in the number of visitors to Canada in the recent past, that has not been so in the case of air visitors from the United States. For example, in the first quarter of 1977 the number of air visitors from the United States to Canada increased by 3.9 per cent. That indicates that use of this particular mode of travel has been on the increase, although there may have been a plateau of the increase in other areas.
On the broader questions of the Excise Tax Act, of the sales tax and of commodity taxation, there was some reference to the statement in the budget that we proposed to have a discussion in the committee of the commodity tax review which was tabled by my predecessor in his second last budget and which has been the subject of much representation by members of the public.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL COMMITTEE EXAMINE UPHOLDING OF HUMAN FREEDOMS UNDER PROVISIONS OF HELSINKI AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That the Helsinki Agreement be referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to obtain evidence of the extent to which States signatory thereto have observed their obligations contained in basket 3 (human freedoms) and that the Commission have power to travel from place to place within Canada to hold public meetings on this matter.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in August, 1975, an historic agreement made by European and North American powers was signed at Helsinki, Finland, settling some questions of security and co-operation. A number of political issues were resolved at Helsinki dealing with questions which remain highly contentious so far as some Canadians are concerned. Some states were not represented by governments of their peoples, or by what we, in our democratic country, consider as governments.
I did not place this motion on the order paper in order to discuss the validity of the Helsinki agreement on those grounds. Actually I am not rising to object to the Helsinki Agreement. On the contrary, I shall address my attention this afternoon to the implementation of the Helsinki Agreement.
In signing the Helsinki Agreement, the Government of Canada has often stressed how important it considers assurances given by other countries of their co-operation in humanitarian and other fields. The undertakings with respect to such co-operation are often referred to as the Basket III provisions of the Helsinki Agreement. In a moment I shall examine some of the issues relating to Basket III to the Helsinki Agreement. Before I do that, let me remind the House of the importance of the issues I intend to raise. Their importance is this: on June 15, 1977, a conference is to be convened in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, to deal with the implementation of the issues I intend to raise. Their importance is this: on June 15, 1977, a conference is to be convened in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, to deal with the implementation of the Helsinki Agreement. I have a copy of the agreement with me and will note and refer in detail to specific undertakings given by states signatory to the Helsinki Agreement as to follow-up. They agreed, on June 15, to
May 20, 1977

declare their resolve, in the period following the conference, to pay due regard to and implement the provisions of the Final Act of the conference unilaterally, in all cases which lend themselves to such action; bilaterally, in all cases which lend themselves to such action; bilaterally, by negotiations with other participating states, and multilaterally. I want to emphasize the agreement which was made that beginning in August, 1975, the members would unilaterally, where they could, implement the undertakings contained in the Helsinki Agreement.
Less than a month from now there will be a meeting in Belgrade, as called for in this document, to review, among other things, the extent to which states have unilaterally implemented the measures and the promises they solemnly made in Helsinki in 1975.
The resolution I tabled last November called for the external affairs committee to travel across Canada receiving briefs from witnesses who would give evidence about the extent to which these undertakings had been observed. If my resolution had been accepted, these hearings would have taken place and the ground work would have been well prepared, but at this point, with less than a month to go, it is hard to imagine that even with the support of the House for the resolution the external affairs committee could carry out such a mandate. Nevertheless, I wish to defend this resolution because 1 assert that if it had been passed in time, and if that tour had taken place, we would be in a much better position at Belgrade in June to deal with the question of the extent to which member states had implemented their undertakings. I wish to refer particularly to the countries of the Soviet Union and the extent to which they have honoured their obligation to carry out unilaterally the promises they formally, solemnly, and in writing agreed upon in Helsinki.
Canada is a country made up of immigrants. I understand that since the Second World War one tenth of all the immigrants who have come to this country have been refugees, often leaving their families. It is typical of immigrants to Canada that they leave members of their families in other parts of the world. So it is proper, totally to be expected, and very Canadian, that this parliament should be concerned about the important question of the reunification of families. In the limited time which I have, I propose to deal with only one small provision in the third basket, the undertaking of the Soviet Union to promote the unification of families, and its agreement that it would unilaterally implement such an undertaking.
If we had inquired across the country we would have learned a great deal. We would have been able to go to Belgrade with many, many cases of both compliance and non-compliance with its undertakings on the part of the Soviet Union. I have many cases before me, partly because I have the honour to represent a very large number of landed immigrants who have come to these shores from the Soviet Union, many of them in the last five or six years. A large number of these have families
Human Freedoms
still living in the Soviet Union and they are asking for the benefit of the Helsinki Agreement.
What is the specific provision to which I should like to draw attention? It is the provision which envisages contacts and regular meetings on the basis of family ties. There are two parts to this. One is an agreement about visiting-family members visiting each other across boundaries. The second has to do with settlement-the right of families to be unified. Let me deal with that briefly.
The Helsinki Agreement provides that in order to promote the further development of contacts on the basis of family ties, participating states will favourably consider applications for travel for the purpose of allowing persons to enter or leave their territory temporarily, and or on a regular basis if desired, in order to visit members of their families. Then there is a reference to the reunification of families where families wish to be reunited permanently. The provision is that the participating states shall deal in a positive and humanitarian spirit with the applications of persons who wish to be reunited with members of their families, with special attention being given to requests of an urgent character.
Dealing with these matters in a positive and humanitarian spirit might, indeed, result in reunification in particular cases. But even with good faith being shown by a government, reunification might not be able to take place. However, the language used there-"dealing in a positive and humanitarian spirit" is quite different from the language used in the case of travel. The participating states say they will favourably consider applications to travel for the purpose of temporary visits.
Let me, then, confine myself to the undertaking of the Soviet Union to consider favourably applications to travel for the purpose of family reunification. In my office alone-and I am only one member of parliament-I have notes of more than a dozen cases of elderly relatives in the Soviet Union who have applied to visit temporarily their relatives in Canada and who have been turned down, in spite of the fact that the Soviet Union was prepared to undertake solemnly that it would favourably consider applications to travel.
I should like to tell the House about just one case, the case of Freda Schafirovich who lives in the Ukraine. She is a widow, 70 years old. She lives alone. Her husband was a war veteran who died defending the Soviet Union against fascist invaders in the Second World War. Not only was her late husband a veteran who served actively and with distinction, but she herself was a war veteran who was wounded in the defence of her city and was honoured for her valiant participation. Perhaps I should say, parenthetically, that the Schafiro-viches were Jewish. When they were defending their country against the fascist invaders they knew what they were defending it against. Perhaps there was never a moment in history when Canadians, Americans, and all free people around the world felt a closer bond than in those terrible days when the Schafiroviches and hundreds and thousands, even millions, of Soviet citizens were rebelling and helping defeat the forces of fascism.

May 20, 1977
Human Freedoms
Mrs. Schafirovich, 70 years old this year, has been trying unsuccessfully for five years to visit her children who live in my constituency in the city of Toronto. Five years ago she received a visa from the Canadian government giving her permission to come to Canada as a temporary visitor, which was all she was asking. She intends to return to the Soviet Union. She applied under the normal procedure for permission from the Soviet authorities to leave that country temporarily. She did not receive a written reply or have anything she could show her son. She was called in and told to forget it, that she would not be allowed to be reunited with her son in Canada.
I have seen Mr. Schafirovich a number of times. I saw him before 1 went to the Soviet Union. When I went to the Soviet Union I had the opportunity of meeting with Chairman Pod-gorny, Chairman of the Supreme Soviet in the Soviet Union. I asked him about Mrs. Frida Shafirovich and when she was going to be allowed to come and visit her son who is living in my constituency, and said she had applied for a temporary visa. He said he would look into it. I understand that Mrs. Schafirovich was called in again. This 70 year old woman, a widow and wounded war veteran, was told to forget it, that she would not be able to visit her son.
Recently a friendly delegation of Soviet parliamentarians came to this country. The son, Arkady Schafirovich, came up to Ottawa and I took him to the Speaker's dining room and introduced him to three or four members of that delegation. They spoke together in Russian and he asked them to see what they could do to get permission for his mother to visit him temporarily in Canada. They took down the details and said they would look into it. They returned home, called in this 70 year old woman and, I understand, told her that she was not going to get to visit Canada to see her son.
I am not a supporter of communism; members of the House know that. But I do know there are many supporters of communism in the world, particularly in the Soviet Union. I should like to know, what does it do for the cause of communism, for socialism as they see it, for the kind of society that they want to establish, to tell a 70 year old Jewish lady, a veteran who fought in the Second World War, that she cannot make a temporary visit to her son?
Since the Schafirovich incident began, a meeting was held at Helsinki. 1 have referred to this one case but there are hundreds, maybe thousands, of Canadians who look to the Helsinki accord for assistance. They do not like the politics of it or the idea of boundaries being drawn around people who were not being democratically represented at the bargaining table when this agreement at Helsinki was settled, but nevertheless, they know about Basket III and they know that the Soviet Union put its signature to an agreement providing that the Soviet Union would favourably consider applications for travel for the purpose of allowing persons to enter or leave their territory temporarily and on a regular basis, at the option of the citizen, in order to visit members of families.
I have told hon. members about the Schafiroviches. I could have told them about a dozen elderly people in the Soviet
(Mr. Kaplan.]
Union who are seeking permission to visit their children in my constituency. There are others who wish to visit their children in other parts of this country, and still others who want to come and settle here, as is also provided for in this agreement. I do not know what the communists are trying to prove. I do not know what possible credit it does to the great revolution which they see themselves as leading when elderly people are now not allowed to be reunited with their children.
1 suppose the most noble and powerful concept I have heard of is the notion of the family of man. We are one family on this planet. We have a responsibility to each other. I believe that the notion of the family of man, this dynamo in the world of ideas, calls upon us to condemn actions like this. I will not be satisfied if the Canadian government goes to Belgrade and fails to bring forward the dozens, indeed hundreds of cases of people who want to visit this country to see their children. I will be very disappointed if the Canadian government goes to that conference and fails to raise the Schafirovich case, as well as the hundreds of other cases where individuals are asking the Soviet Union for permission to visit relatives.
Let us forget about the declaration of human rights, Mr. Speaker-an impressive document, but perhaps it is too stale for the Soviet Union these days. Let us just talk about the Helsinki Agreement and the simple black and white undertakings made at that time to recognize the nature of the family of man.
I cannot say that I will be disappointed if the government prevents this resolution which 1 have proposed today from coming to a vote. I understand the difficulties it would entail at this late date to launch a parliamentary committee across the country to hear from all the Schafiroviches, not just the ones in my riding but those right across the country. I wish the government had of its own initiative, when this idea was first raised, organized that kind of participation by the Canadian people. But I am not going to criticize the government for that decision because I want to wait and see what it does at Belgrade when the Helsinki Agreement is reconsidered. I want to see what kind of evidence is put forward of the extent to which the signatory states to the Helsinki Agreement have observed their undertakings. I see my time has expired, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL COMMITTEE EXAMINE UPHOLDING OF HUMAN FREEDOMS UNDER PROVISIONS OF HELSINKI AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was glad to be asked to speak for my party on this motion. It says something about parliamentary time, as the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) has said, that events have caught up with the purport of his motion. However, 1 am not quite as discouraged as he seems to be about the Department of External Affairs and the list within that department of people who have been brought to the department's attention by members of parliament, and by families from one end of the country to the other. As a matter of fact the department gave a most extraordinarily frank statement to the external affairs committee on Basket III and the monitoring system that has been set up as a result of the Helsinki Agreement.
The particularly moving story that our colleague has reported concerning the mother of a constituent of his and his
May 20, 1977

question about why the might of the Soviet Union should be brought to bear on a 70 year old widow seems to me a matter that we must continue to raise. We can all cite examples of this sort of thing.
The Soviet Union and its government is frightened by the concept of freedom. It is frightened by the concept that mothers can visit their sons in other parts of the world. It is frightened by the concept that a journalist can go to and fro within that country. Its satellite countries are busily locking up journalists, including Canadian journalists, who dare report on the move toward freedom. We cheer, as freedom lovers all over the world cheer, when we learn about the catalogue of heroes coming forth to speak out against totalitarian regimes. This is the antithesis of the Soviet system, that huge country known as the super power. It has, as senior officials of its government, parliamentarians who are the sycophants of that government. They are elected from a list and know no dissent. That group is unable to cope with the simple act of family reunification. I do not mean to be self-righteous, and God knows we have our difficulties, but it would not take a group of members of this House to see to it that sons can visit mothers and mothers visit sons, or families have an opportunity to get together.
I feel rather hopeful about Helsinki, if we keep the truth in front of the world. I think the human rights basket was made a condition of the eastern bloc being able to institutionalize the boundaries of the Second World War.
Members of parliament and agencies of government have to keep on monitoring occasions when undertakings in Basket III are not fulfilled by the signatories to this treaty. I am sad to think there will be many such occasions. Our hon. friend has given us an example and he has said there are many others. Parliamentarians from all parties have raised this from time to time. We should have the opportunity to think beyond the boundaries of our country occasionally. This is an illustration that we can do this once in a while.
We think of names like Valentyn Moroz, a man who is being held now because the Soviet Union cannot stand having a Christian preaching the gospel. Imagine the whole engine of the state of the Soviet Union quivering, and putting a man in jail because he professes his belief. I am somewhat optimistic about Basket III. We do not need, in espousing the cause of human rights, to overstate the case. The case is well stated in hundreds of precedents through the United Nations and other times in history when men have espoused the cause of human rights.
The Belgrade meeting next month is embarrassed by Basket III. The Soviet bloc do not want to discuss the things which our colleague has been discussing today. They would rather forget the people within their boundaries who cannot see their sons, and forget the people they have put in jail because of their beliefs. I am anxious for us not to get into the language of the Cold War, which was a particularly trying time for freedom lovers. I know we all have the perspective of looking back, but it seems to me some things were done in the western
Human Freedoms
world which echoed the intolerance of the Soviets. It was not echoed in totality, but they did echo some of the statements and techniques which are now being used in the Soviet Union and its satellites. We should keep telling the truth.
Our hon. friend has introduced sections of the Helsinki Agreement into this debate. There are examples of human beings who have suffered because the agreement was not lived up to by others. We cannot continue stating the case without trying to roll back communism and going to the brink, and some people are prepared to go to the brink. We should not use the outlandish phrases of the fifties. The brink I am referring to is not only in intellectual terms but the brink of their thinking. Perhaps I have not put that too well. What I am trying to say is that we have the case on our side in the sense that the document is there. If the document is not fulfilled, we should tell the world so.
When the departmental officials and the minister go to Belgrade, they should take the entire Helsinki Agreement with them. We should never consider going to Belgrade without it. We cannot be selective in the western world and agree to look at parts of that agreement. We have to look at the complete agreement.
Despite Berlin walls, despite all the boundaries, and despite the suspicion of the eastern bloc, mankind's ingenuity in technological terms is soon going to surmount this in freedom of information. Whether the Soviet Union likes it or not, we are on the threshold of developing a system of receiving information via satellites. That is going to confound boundaries and confound suspicious people who head totalitarian regimes. Although families may not be reunited, in the future there will be information about the west-how the west lives, and how we care very deeply about the thousands of cases which are caught under the basket of the human rights provisions. People who want to find out the truth can get the truth in technological terms. We are in a curious situation because some technology seems to be the antithesis of humanity. However, humanity is well served in this case because all people do inhabit a global home, and technology is going to make this known to all the inhabitants of the earth. The inhabitants of the earth are going to know when a super power is unable to let a 70 year old woman visit her son.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL COMMITTEE EXAMINE UPHOLDING OF HUMAN FREEDOMS UNDER PROVISIONS OF HELSINKI AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will probably recall that the Final Act of Helsinki was signed on August 1, 1975. It is a unique document in many respects. It is the result of a process which, from the outset, the Soviet Union only meant to be a simple effort to obtain international recognition of the status quo in post-war Europe, but which led to a conference dealing with much broader problems: the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe. Not only did that conference reiterate established principles which acknowledged the possibility of changes in inter-state relations, but it also gave a humani-
5870

May 20, 1977
Human Freedoms
tarian scope to those relations. It considered human rights and each state's treatment of its own citizens as issues which are not only negotiable, but also likely to influence international relations.
In the first basket of the final agreement, principle VII of the "Declaration on Principles Guiding Relations between Participating States" is particularly enlightening in that regard. I quote:
The participating states recognize the universal significance of human rights and fundamental freedoms, respect for which is an essential factor for the peace, justice and well-being necessary to ensure the development of friendly relations and co-operation among themselves as among all states.
This principle was agreed upon thanks to the perseverance of the western nations, as well as the provisions contained in the third basket on "Co-operation in humanitarian and other fields", which deal with some specific aspects of human rights, as for example the free circulation of persons and the free diffusion of information. Hon. members will undoubtedly recall that the Canadian delegation in Geneva put forward the proposition which is the basis for the provision contained in the third basket about the reunification of families. One must not wonder why Canada is interested.
I wish to draw hon. members' attention on the content of the third basket, which is the subject of the motion before us. It does not contain the basic declaration of the final act, respecting human rights, which is to be found rather in principle VII of the first basket, as I already said.
As for the third basket, it deals with certain points which I enumerate in detail to avoid any confusion with the provisions of a more general nature contained in the first basket as far as human rights are concerned:
1.	Human contacts namely:
(a)	contacts and regular meetings on the basis of family ties;
(b)	reunification of families;
(c)	marriage between citizens of different states;
(d)	travel for personal or professional reasons;
(e)	improvement of conditions for tourism on an individual or collective basis;
(0 meetings among young people; and
(g) sport.
2.	Information, namely:
(a)	improvement of the circulation of, access to, and exchange of information
(not only oral but also printed, filmed and broadcast information);
(b)	co-operation in the field of information; and
(c)	improvement of working conditions for journalists.
3.	Culture, i.e. contacts and exchanges in the fields of cinema, theatre, music, opera, ballet, plastic and graphic arts, books, copyrights, translation, etc.
4.	Education, i.e. fields of activity like science, foreign languages and civilizations, and teaching methods.
In view of the large interest those aspects of the final act have for the Canadian public, it is important to know what are its views on them. In fact, it is essential that the Canadian delegation to the meeting subsequent to the CSCE, to be held in Belgrade later this year, be fully aware of the Canadian public's position with regard to the CSCE and the third basket, and have all the factual information which can be provided to them by individuals as well as organizations.

The government has been receiving mail on that matter for quite some time already. Almost every letter relates to the way countries of Eastern Europe are behaving. In some cases, they do not provide for any precise information and they even go as far as accusing some countries of violating sections of the final act of Helsinki which do not even exist. What the Canadian delegation needs is precise, accurate and well documented information.
During a meeting with leaders of the allophone communities in Toronto held February last, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) invited them to express their points of view and to meet senior officials in his department. Some verbal statements and written briefs have already been presented not only to high officials but to the minister himself. We are expecting some more.
The views of the allophone communities represent, of course, only a part of a larger group and the Department of External Affairs is open to any kinds of contributions. Incidentally, he has recently invited some representatives of the university community in Ottawa in order to hear their views on the application of the final act of Belgrade.
The department also receives on a regular basis some information on the compliance with the final act by other countries from other Canadian departments, from its missions abroad and from all those, including high officials, who took part in what is in fact a continuous process of consultations between the signatories to the CSCE and the final act. One can say in that regard that process was initiated right after Helsinki and was followed up since then on a continuous basis.
Right in our department, a small section was established a few years ago to get ready for the CSCE and co-ordinate the activities of various governmental services in that area. It also dealt with the way Canada is itself complying with the provisions of the Final Act.

In view of the extensive activity already being carried out by the government, there is some question whether there might not be a certain duplication of effort in having the standing committee take on a similar activity, especially at this time.
The motion under consideration should be considered in the context of the present heavy workload of parliamentary committees and the responsibilities they are already called upon to discharge before the end of the current session. I have been informed that at least 12 bills must be considered by six or seven committees in the next month. With such a load on hon. members' time and committee resources, a thorough and useful investigation by the standing committee would be difficult to hold in Ottawa, and next to impossible to hold in all parts of the country. I feel that the aims of the motion are laudable, but pragmatic questions of logistics must be considered.
Preparatory meetings begin in Belgrade in less than one month, on June 15, and the main meeting is scheduled for October of this year. We are dealing with very serious issues here. There is a real danger that committee hearings at this
May 20, 1977

time, and within these time constraints, would be hasty, incomplete, and superficial.
The preparatory organization of the committee's work, the actual hearings, the verification of information, the follow-up work, and the necessary co-ordination with the Department of External Affairs-all these essentials steps make it doubtful that hearings envisaged under the motion could make the practical, positive contribution to our representations at Belgrade at which we should be aiming.
There is another very important point which I have not yet touched on, and that is the limited scope of the motion. I fully appreciate the reason why attention has been focused on Basket III, but it should be borne in mind that there are many subjects covered by the Final Act, and just as Canadians may be interested in only certain aspects of the document, others will be interested in different parts. We cannot afford to ignore those other parts. All the principles have to be read in conjunction with each other, and the three substantive baskets of the Final Act have to be read together, particularly as the commitment of the Canadian government is to the whole Final Act and not just to Basket III.
Hearings which concentrated only on Basket III would fail to come to grips will all the problems which will have to be faced at Belgrade. At the same time, if the standing committee were to do a proper job on the whole Final Act, the task it would have to take on would be an enormous one to try to accomplish within the time frame allowed. I put these thoughts forward for the consideration of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a moment so that the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) can still make his contribution. I should simply like to say that even though events since last November may have overtaken the precise suggestions contained in the motion put down by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), I want to join in congratulating him for having presented this motion and making possible the discussion which has taken place this afternoon.
Human rights everywhere in the world are of deep concern to all of us. It is a subject about which we must speak out when those rights are violated, and on behalf of my party I support very strongly the spirit and the intention which led the hon. member to put this motion down for debate today.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be equally brief, and I thank the hon. member for allowing me to have a few moments. I see that the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) would also like to speak.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) for bringing forward this motion. I regret that time has telescoped on us so much, but this Belgrade conference was only one of what surely must be many, and I think the idea that a reference be made to that committee is a sound one. I think too that we ought to state in this House that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) should
Human Freedoms
include in the delegation going to Belgrade some representatives of the House of Commons so that we at the political level will know what is going on there, and so that we can assess the progress of our own efforts to pressure for progress in that respect. I think too that we should have representatives at Belgrade from non-governmental organizations, and that they in turn should include Canadian citizens who have come from those countries which are denying family reunifications and visits: the U.S.S.R., Czechoslovakia, Poland and others.
We are having our noses rubbed into the Helsinki Agreement, principally by the U.S.S.R. but not just by it. Why can we say that? Well, our government signed the agreement. That agreement included pledges that Canadian citizens would receive visits from their relatives behind the Iron Curtain and that those visits would be facilitated. I too have dozens of such cases in my office. I have not had one success as a result of my representations. We are having our noses rubbed into the agreement which we signed. We were party to it, and therefore I think it is in our interest to negotiate criteria at Belgrade which would ensure that we can respond to citizens. Therefore, I think we ought to be represented at Belgrade.
Mr. Speaker, I will yield to the hon. member for Trinity.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL COMMITTEE EXAMINE UPHOLDING OF HUMAN FREEDOMS UNDER PROVISIONS OF HELSINKI AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since there are only a few minutes left before the time for this debate ends, I just want to say very briefly that I support the intent of the motion of the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan). Because the inclusion of Basket III in the Helsinki Final Act was a Canadian initiative, we have a particular responsibility to monitor it. Like other hon. members who have spoken, I hear daily from my constituents of countless examples of people who cannot come here for a simple family visit, about elderly and sick people who cannot be reunited, although that was a specific recommendation in the Final Act and about unconscionable interference with the mails, with gifts and with these simple matters which help families to keep in touch.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) in his usual thoughtful way reminded us of the importance of conducting our negotiations at Belgrade in a way which is not counterproductive, which does not involve unnecessary confrontation, and which keeps the emphasis on the whole agreement, not just on Basket III. I think his point is well taken, but I also think Canadians know a lot about how to make a point firmly but politely. We can keep the door open for negotiation, but we must also state very clearly the cases and examples of blatant interference with the rights of people in their own countries which we know.
Some of the worst abuses of human rights now are perpetrated by governments against their own nationals, and while we cannot interfere with the internal matters of other countries, in the Helsinki Final Act some 35 governments have voluntarily taken a position and made a commitment. With this important agreement we can continue to expect governments to be accountable for that to which they have committed themselves.
